Issued at 310 AM EST Thu Nov 12 2026

Early this morning GFS 500mb height analysis showed an elongated 
upper level low pressure over Quebec and Newfoundland. Shortwaves 
were rotating around the low with a more well defined shortwave over 
the Upper Great Lakes. This shortwave was also evident in the GOES-R 
water vapor imagery, spinning over the U.P. Surface observations 
showed temperatures had cooled into the low 30s for the inland areas 
of the western and central U.P. with mid 30s near Lake Superior and 
the eastern U.P. where relatively warm lake waters were modifying 
the airmass. Satellite and radar showed snow showers over much of 
the western and northern half of the U.P. Snow was struggling to 
stick on concrete surfaces but webcams did show periods of slushy 
conditions during heavier snow showers over the higher elevations of 
Marquette and Baraga counties. 

The primary forecast concern continues to be the lake effect snow 
potential through Saturday. A Winter Weather Advisory is in effect 
through 1200 EDT Friday as the high terrain of Baraga and Marquette 
Counties is still expected to see 3"-8" of snow throughout the next 
2 days.

Through Saturday shortwaves will dive south through the Upper Great 
Lakes, around the back side of the upper low over Quebec, helping to 
maintain moisture, cooler temps and lake effect snow showers. 850mb 
temperatures this morning were in the -6 to -8C range, plenty 
sufficient for LES given Lake Superior water temperatures are in the 
8-10C range. 

The main challenges with this forecast continue to be 
temperatures, snow ratios, precip intensity (QPF) and the resulting 
accumulations when combining the QPF and snow ratios. While the 
current forecast of 3-8" above 1000' elevation (or about 400-600+ ft 
above Lake Superior) is still on the lower end of traditional 
criteria for a 48 hour span, the wet/slushy nature of the snow (at 
least initially) and expected occasional moderate-to-heavy rates 
(0.5-1.0+"/hr) support the first advisory of the 2026-27 winter 
season. Near the Lake Superior shoreline, warm flow onshore from an 
above-freezing Lake Superior will result in generally less than an 
inch of accumulation (including the city of Marquette). The best 
chance to see any accumulations there would be Thursday night when 
the 850mb temps fall to near -9C (REFS mean). Impacts to the area 
roads will be greatest during the overnight hours, though periods of 
heavier snow during the daylight hours will still be impactful. 

For snow ratios and intensity, frictional convergence over the 
terrain of the western and north central U.P. have largely 
contributed to the development of snow showers thus far but banding 
has become more prevalent over the last hour with the passing 
shortwave trough axis. Expecting this trend to continue as 
convergent flow develops over the eastern 2/3 of the lake. 
Thermodynamic profiles have shown an overall lack of moisture in the 
DGZ (mainly snow pellets / riming was being observed overnight). Low 
level moisture is expected to deepen as well this morning. CAM 
(HRRR/ RRFS) simulated reflectivity align with this as they show 
rather well defined bands forming by mid-morning along with an 
uptick in intensity. SLRs continue to be overdone in the NBM with 
16:1 by Friday including over the Great Lakes. High snow ratios are 
unlikely given the warmer low levels and warm ground temperatures 
(mid 40s) ongoing. Similar thermal profiles to last week's high 
terrain lake effect snowfall yielded between 5:1 and 7:1 SLR. These 
values seem reasonable for today, then approach 10:1 tonight as 
cooling continues. A locally developed temperature-to-SLR curve 
matches up well with this for areas away from the lake. Have largely 
maintained the SLRs from previous shifts. Notably REFS soundings 
interior from the Great Lakes do show inversion heights to around 8-
9kft and saturation into the DGZ, which would support periods of 
above 10:1 SLRs (without the above context of warmer temperatures, 
etc) in heavier bands.

For temperatures, the NBM continues to forecast much too cold for 
overnight temperatures as its bias-correction has been trained on 
recent stretches of cool, clear nights. This results in it having 
temperatures falling into the mid 20s over the interior and even 
below freezing at the immediate lakeshore tonight and Friday night. 
This is unlikely given the strong onshore flow from a warm lake, 
cloud cover, precipitation processes releasing latent heat, and only 
marginally cold 850mb temps of -8 to -10C. Overall thinking is that 
temperatures will remain above freezing near the Lake Superior 
shoreline and much of the eastern U.P. through Friday night, thus 
limiting snow accumulations there.
